title: CDN Caching Strategies
description: Learn how Content Delivery Networks reduce latency and improve availability through edge caching.

data.text: A Content Delivery Network, or CDN, is a globally distributed network of proxy servers that cache content close to end users. Instead of every request traveling all the way to your origin server, a CDN serves cached copies from a nearby edge location. This dramatically reduces latency, cuts origin bandwidth costs, and improves resilience against traffic spikes.

When a user requests a resource such as an image, stylesheet, or API response, the CDN checks whether it already has a fresh cached copy. If it does, the edge node returns the cached response immediately. If not, the CDN fetches the content from the origin server, caches it according to the configured TTL, and then serves it to the user. Subsequent requests for the same content are then served from the cache until the entry expires or is invalidated.

data.title: Core CDN Concepts:
items: TTL: Time-to-live determines how long a cached object remains fresh before the CDN revalidates with the origin.
Cache key: The combination of URL, headers, and cookies used to identify a unique cached entry.
Purge vs invalidate: Purge removes content immediately, while invalidation marks it stale so the next request fetches a fresh copy.
Origin shield: An additional caching layer between edge nodes and the origin that reduces origin load.

data.title: Interview Tip
data.text: Mention that CDNs excel at static assets and read-heavy workloads. For dynamic or personalized content, discuss edge computing, cache-key customization, or origin-shield patterns to reduce origin pressure.

rows: Simple, but requires cache busting on updates
Higher hit rate, but cache keys must avoid personalization leaks
Lower latency, but cold starts can add variance

data.text: In system design interviews, discussing CDNs signals that you understand global scale and user experience. You should mention geographic distribution, cache hit ratio as a key metric, and the importance of cache-control headers. If the system has real-time data requirements, explain how short TTLs or cache bypass headers keep content fresh while still offloading the majority of traffic from the origin.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: CDNs serve cached content from edge locations near users
TTL, cache keys, and purge controls determine cache freshness
CDNs reduce latency, bandwidth cost, and origin load
Choose strategies based on content type and freshness requirements
data.takeaway: A strong CDN strategy combines global edge placement with careful cache-control policies to balance performance and data freshness.

items.question: When should I use a CDN?
items.answer: Use a CDN for static assets, public APIs, and globally distributed read-heavy workloads. Even dynamic sites benefit from CDN offloading for images, scripts, and stylesheets.

items.question: What is the difference between cache hit and cache miss?
items.answer: A cache hit occurs when the CDN has a fresh cached copy and returns it directly. A cache miss happens when the CDN must fetch the content from the origin server before serving it.
